difficultyReason: The stimulus presents mixed quantitative data with a key qualification about a subgroup. The correct answer respects those qualifications with hedged language. Traps include one absolute claim and one that drops the subgroup qualifier.
stimulus: A clinical review of 4,200 patients treated for hypertension at regional hospitals found that patients who adhered to low-sodium diets reduced their systolic blood pressure by an average of 11 mmHg over six months. However, among patients who were also prescribed diuretics, dietary sodium reduction produced an average systolic reduction of only 3 mmHg — roughly one-quarter the effect seen in the broader group. Patients with chronic kidney disease were excluded from the analysis because their sodium metabolism differs markedly from that of the general hypertensive population.
questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Low-sodium diets are the most effective single intervention for reducing systolic blood pressure in hypertensive patients.

choices.label: B
choices.text: For at least some hypertensive patients taking diuretics, a low-sodium diet produces a smaller reduction in systolic blood pressure than it does for hypertensive patients not taking diuretics.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Diuretics cancel out all of the blood-pressure benefits of a low-sodium diet in hypertensive patients.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patients with chronic kidney disease would show no improvement in blood pressure from a low-sodium diet.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hypertensive patients who are not prescribed diuretics should always adopt low-sodium diets before any other treatment is attempted.

explanations.correct: The data directly show that diuretic patients averaged only 3 mmHg reduction versus 11 mmHg for the broader group, so there are hypertensive patients on diuretics for whom the dietary effect is smaller. The hedged 'at least some' accurately captures this without overclaiming.
explanations.A: Too strong and unsupported — the stimulus makes no comparison between sodium restriction and other interventions.
explanations.B: Correct. The comparative data directly support this hedged inference.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'cancel out all' goes beyond the data, which show a diminished but still present effect (3 mmHg).
explanations.D: Opposite direction / unsupported — kidney disease patients were excluded precisely because their sodium metabolism differs; the stimulus does not say they would receive no benefit.
explanations.E: Too strong and normative — 'always' and 'before any other treatment' are not supported by the data.

difficultyReason: The stimulus contains a counterintuitive economic finding with a temporal qualification. Traps exploit the tendency to generalize across all time periods or to invert the direction of the finding.
stimulus: Data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics covering the period 1980–2022 show that in years when the national unemployment rate rose by more than two percentage points, consumer spending on live entertainment — concerts, theater, and sporting events — declined by an average of 8 percent. During the same years, however, consumer spending on home entertainment technology, including streaming subscriptions and gaming hardware, rose by an average of 14 percent. In years of stable or declining unemployment, no consistent pattern emerged between unemployment and either category of entertainment spending.
questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Consumers always substitute home entertainment for live entertainment when economic conditions worsen.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Live entertainment is a luxury good, while home entertainment technology is a necessity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: During periods of sharply rising unemployment, spending on home entertainment technology has tended to increase even as spending on live entertainment has declined.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rising unemployment causes consumers to spend less on all discretionary goods.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Home entertainment and live entertainment are always in direct economic competition with one another.

explanations.correct: The data establish that in years of sharp unemployment increases, live entertainment spending fell while home entertainment spending rose. The hedged 'has tended to' accurately reflects the pattern without overclaiming causation or universality.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'always' is not justified; the data cover specific conditions (unemployment rises >2 points), not all economic downturns.
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported — the luxury/necessity economic classification is not derivable from these spending patterns alone.
explanations.C: Correct. Directly summarizes the documented pattern with appropriately hedged language.
explanations.D: Too strong and out of scope — the data don't address all discretionary goods, only two entertainment categories.
explanations.E: Too strong — 'always' and 'direct economic competition' go beyond what the data support; no consistent pattern was found in stable/declining unemployment years.

difficultyReason: The environmental science stimulus presents multiple data points with a specific geographic qualifier. The correct answer draws a modest comparative inference; traps either drop the geographic qualifier or make an absolute causal claim.
stimulus: Water quality monitoring conducted along three major river systems in the Pacific Northwest between 2010 and 2023 detected elevated concentrations of microplastic particles in reaches located downstream of urban centers, with median concentrations approximately six times higher than in upstream reaches of the same rivers. Agricultural reaches — those running primarily through farmland rather than urban areas — showed median microplastic concentrations intermediate between upstream and urban-downstream readings. Testing methodology was standardized across all sampling sites.
questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Urban centers are the sole source of microplastic contamination in Pacific Northwest river systems.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Microplastic concentrations in these rivers tend to be higher in reaches near urban centers than in reaches near agricultural areas.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reducing plastic use in urban areas would eliminate microplastic pollution in downstream river reaches.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Agricultural runoff contains no microplastic particles.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Microplastic concentrations in all rivers worldwide are higher downstream of urban areas than downstream of agricultural areas.

explanations.correct: The data establish that urban-downstream reaches had the highest median concentrations and agricultural reaches had intermediate concentrations, directly supporting the hedged comparative claim in B.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'sole source' is not supported; agricultural reaches also showed elevated concentrations.
explanations.B: Correct. Directly follows from the comparison of median concentrations between urban-downstream and agricultural reaches.
explanations.C: Too strong — the data don't address what elimination of plastic use would achieve, nor do they identify reduction as sufficient.
explanations.D: Contradicted by the data — agricultural reaches had intermediate (elevated) concentrations, implying some microplastic presence.
explanations.E: Scope creep — the data cover three Pacific Northwest rivers only; extending the claim to 'all rivers worldwide' is unsupported.

difficultyReason: The linguistics stimulus presents a specific observational finding with a clear exception. Traps include overgeneralizing to all languages and inverting the directionality.
stimulus: Linguists studying phoneme acquisition in bilingual children aged two to four found that children exposed to two languages from birth reached phonemic milestones — the ability to consistently distinguish and produce the distinct sounds of each language — at roughly the same age as monolingual peers for each individual language, though they showed greater variability in milestone timing. Children who began regular exposure to a second language after age two, however, showed consistent delays of three to five months in producing phonemes unique to the second language, delays not observed for their first language.
questionStem: Which one of the following inferences is most supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bilingual children are generally slower to develop language skills than monolingual children.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The age at which a child first receives regular exposure to a language can affect how quickly that child acquires phonemes specific to that language.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Children who learn two languages from birth will eventually outperform monolingual children on all phonemic tasks.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Delays in phoneme acquisition for a second language necessarily indicate a broader cognitive deficit.

choices.label: E
choices.text: After age two, no child can fully acquire the phonemic system of a second language.

explanations.correct: The contrast between from-birth bilinguals (no delays) and late-exposure bilinguals (3–5 month delays in the second language's unique phonemes) directly supports the inference that timing of exposure influences phoneme acquisition speed.
explanations.A: Opposite direction — the data show from-birth bilinguals reach milestones at roughly the same age as monolinguals for each language; this answer misrepresents the finding.
explanations.B: Correct. The observed delay in late-exposure children but not in from-birth bilinguals strongly supports this modest causal inference.
explanations.C: Too strong and unsupported — the data show similar milestone timing, not eventual superiority.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported — the stimulus provides no information about broader cognitive deficits.
explanations.E: Too strong — 'no child can fully acquire' is an absolute claim not supported by data that show delays, not permanent incapacity.

difficultyReason: The policy stimulus contains two findings that are in mild tension; the correct answer draws a modest, qualified inference that respects both findings. Traps exploit the tension by treating one finding as absolute.
stimulus: A statewide evaluation of mandatory minimum sentencing laws found that counties that adopted such laws saw a 12 percent average reduction in the targeted offense categories during the first two years of implementation. Over a ten-year period, however, the same counties showed no statistically significant difference in those offense rates compared with counties that had not adopted mandatory minimums. Jurisdictions that paired mandatory minimums with funded rehabilitation programs showed sustained reductions — averaging 9 percent — over the full ten-year period.
questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mandatory minimum sentencing laws, on their own, may not produce lasting reductions in targeted offense rates.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mandatory minimum sentencing laws always increase public safety in the short term.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rehabilitation programs alone are sufficient to reduce crime rates in any jurisdiction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Counties that did not adopt mandatory minimums experienced rising offense rates over the ten-year period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The short-term reduction in offense rates caused by mandatory minimums is entirely due to incapacitation of offenders.

explanations.correct: The ten-year data show no significant difference between mandatory-minimum and non-mandatory-minimum counties, while paired programs did produce sustained results. This supports the inference that mandatory minimums alone may not sustain reductions — a properly hedged claim.
explanations.A: Correct. The ten-year convergence in offense rates directly supports this modest, hedged conclusion.
explanations.B: Too strong — 'always' overstates the finding; the 12% reduction is an average, not a universal outcome.
explanations.C: Too strong and out of scope — the data address paired programs, not rehabilitation programs alone; 'any jurisdiction' is unsupported.
explanations.D: Unsupported — 'no statistically significant difference' doesn't tell us that comparison counties saw rising rates; they may have been stable.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported — the mechanism behind the short-term reduction is not addressed in the data.

difficultyReason: The technology stimulus presents a specific engineering finding with a narrow domain qualifier. The correct answer draws a hedged comparative inference; traps either widen the domain or reverse the direction of the finding.
stimulus: Engineers testing lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) and nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) battery cells under simulated rapid-charging conditions found that LFP cells retained approximately 91 percent of their original capacity after 2,000 charge cycles, while NMC cells retained approximately 74 percent under the same conditions. Both cell types performed comparably — within two percentage points — in tests involving standard overnight charging. The tests were conducted at a uniform temperature of 25°C; performance at higher temperatures was not evaluated.
questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: LFP batteries last longer than NMC batteries under all real-world usage conditions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Under rapid-charging conditions, LFP cells tend to degrade more slowly than NMC cells.

choices.label: C
choices.text: NMC batteries are inferior to LFP batteries for all commercial applications.

choices.label: D
choices.text: At elevated temperatures, LFP cells retain more capacity than NMC cells after 2,000 rapid-charge cycles.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Standard overnight charging destroys battery capacity more quickly than rapid charging in both LFP and NMC cells.

explanations.correct: The rapid-charging test data directly show LFP retained 91% versus NMC's 74% after 2,000 cycles, supporting the hedged claim that LFP degrades more slowly under those conditions.
explanations.A: Too strong and scope creep — 'all real-world usage conditions' is unsupported; standard charging showed comparable performance.
explanations.B: Correct. Directly supported by the rapid-charging cycle data with appropriately hedged language.
explanations.C: Too strong — the data don't address all commercial applications, and standard charging performance was comparable.
explanations.D: Unsupported — the stimulus explicitly states elevated temperature performance was not evaluated.
explanations.E: Opposite direction — the data don't compare overnight vs. rapid charging degradation rates; overnight charging showed comparable performance, not faster degradation.

difficultyReason: The history stimulus involves a documented correlation with a temporal scope limitation. The correct answer is a modest hedged inference; traps either extend the scope or posit unsupported causal mechanisms.
stimulus: Records from Mediterranean port cities during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries show that periods of prolonged drought in the North African interior, lasting three or more consecutive years, were followed within five years by measurable increases in the volume of grain shipped into those port cities from Iberian and Italian sources. Shorter droughts — lasting one to two years — show no consistent correlation with shifts in grain import volumes. Shipping records from Northern European ports during the same period do not display the same pattern.
questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Prolonged drought in North Africa during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries sometimes coincided with increased grain imports to Mediterranean port cities.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Short droughts in North Africa had no effect on agricultural output during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mediterranean port cities depended entirely on North African grain supplies during drought years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The same relationship between North African drought and grain trade patterns held throughout all European port cities in this period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Northern European grain merchants were unaffected by Mediterranean climate conditions during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

explanations.correct: The records establish a documented correlation between prolonged droughts (3+ years) and increased grain imports to Mediterranean ports within five years — supporting the hedged 'sometimes coincided' formulation, which accurately reflects the pattern without asserting causation.
explanations.A: Correct. 'Sometimes' and 'coincided' are appropriately hedged; the data directly document the correlation.
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported — the data show no consistent correlation with import volumes, but this doesn't mean short droughts had no effect on agricultural output; those are different measures.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'entirely' is unsupported; the data show increased imports, not total dependence.
explanations.D: Scope creep and opposite direction — the stimulus explicitly states Northern European ports did not show the same pattern.
explanations.E: Too strong and plausible-but-unsupported — 'unaffected' is an absolute claim; the data only address grain import volume patterns, not all possible effects.

difficultyReason: The ethics/policy stimulus presents survey data on moral reasoning with a specific demographic qualifier. Traps exploit either the demographic qualifier or the direction of the finding.
stimulus: A survey of 1,800 adults asked respondents to evaluate the moral acceptability of five types of deception — ranging from white lies to fraud — in professional contexts. Among respondents who identified as having frequent direct client contact in their work, approximately 68 percent rated at least one form of deception as morally acceptable in certain professional circumstances. Among respondents in administrative roles with minimal client contact, that figure was 41 percent. The survey did not control for respondents' professional field.
questionStem: Which one of the following inferences is most supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: People who interact directly with clients are more likely to regard at least some professional deception as morally acceptable than are people in administrative roles.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Client-facing professionals are more likely to engage in deceptive behavior than administrative workers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most adults believe that all forms of deception are morally unacceptable in professional contexts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Professional field is the primary determinant of attitudes toward deception in the workplace.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Administrative employees universally oppose deception, while client-facing employees universally accept it.

explanations.correct: The data directly show 68% of client-contact respondents vs. 41% of administrative respondents rated at least one form of deception as acceptable — a straightforward comparative inference with no overclaiming.
explanations.A: Correct. Directly reflects the percentage comparison between the two groups, hedged by 'more likely.'
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported — the survey measures attitudes, not actual behavior; inferring behavior from reported moral attitudes is not warranted by the data.
explanations.C: Opposite direction — the data show majorities or large minorities of both groups accepting some deception, contradicting this claim.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported — the survey explicitly did not control for professional field, so this causal primacy claim cannot be derived.
explanations.E: Too strong — 'universally' is contradicted by the data (32% of client-facing and 59% of administrative respondents did not rate any deception as acceptable).

difficultyReason: The arts stimulus presents critical reception data with a period qualification. Traps include absolute claims about artistic quality and a scope-creep error extending findings beyond the stated period.
stimulus: An analysis of critical reviews published in major English-language periodicals between 1950 and 1975 found that works by composers who had trained under the serialist tradition received substantially fewer favorable reviews — averaging 2.1 favorable per composer per decade — than works by composers associated with neo-Romantic styles, who averaged 5.8 favorable reviews per composer per decade. After 1975, the gap in favorable review rates between the two groups narrowed considerably, with serialist composers averaging 4.3 and neo-Romantic composers averaging 5.1 favorable reviews per composer per decade.
questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Between 1950 and 1975, serialist composers tended to receive less favorable critical attention in major English-language periodicals than neo-Romantic composers did.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Serialist music is objectively less artistically meritorious than neo-Romantic music.

choices.label: C
choices.text: After 1975, critical reception of serialist music exceeded that of neo-Romantic music in major English-language periodicals.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Critical opinion of serialist music has always been negative in English-language publications.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The same pattern of critical reception holds for non-English-language periodicals during both periods.

explanations.correct: The data directly support a comparative claim about favorable review rates during the 1950–1975 period, and 'tended to receive' hedges appropriately against treating averages as universal rules.
explanations.A: Correct. Directly summarizes the pre-1975 comparison (2.1 vs. 5.8 favorable reviews per decade) with hedged language.
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported — critical reception data measure reviewer preferences, not objective artistic merit; the link between the two is not established.
explanations.C: Opposite direction — after 1975, neo-Romantic composers still averaged more favorable reviews (5.1) than serialist composers (4.3); the gap narrowed but did not reverse.
explanations.D: Too strong — 'always been negative' is not supported; after 1975 serialists averaged 4.3 favorable reviews per decade, which is not a negative reception.
explanations.E: Scope creep — the analysis covered only major English-language periodicals; extending to non-English publications is unsupported.

difficultyReason: The environmental science/economics stimulus presents data with a counterintuitive finding about a specific regulatory mechanism. Traps include an absolute causal claim, a scope error, and a reversal of the finding's direction.
stimulus: An economic analysis of cap-and-trade programs implemented in twelve jurisdictions between 1995 and 2020 found that industries covered by these programs reduced their emissions by an average of 19 percent over ten years. Industries in the same jurisdictions that were exempt from cap-and-trade but subject to flat-rate emissions taxes reduced their emissions by an average of 11 percent over the same period. However, in three of the twelve jurisdictions — those where permit prices fell below a threshold of $15 per ton — covered industries showed no statistically significant emissions reduction.
questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cap-and-trade programs are, in at least some jurisdictions, associated with greater emissions reductions than flat-rate emissions taxes over a ten-year period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flat-rate emissions taxes always produce smaller emissions reductions than cap-and-trade programs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cap-and-trade programs universally reduce emissions regardless of permit price levels.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the three jurisdictions where permit prices fell below $15 per ton, flat-rate taxes also failed to reduce emissions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Emissions taxes produce greater reductions than cap-and-trade programs when permit prices are low.

explanations.correct: Across the twelve jurisdictions overall, cap-and-trade averaged 19% versus 11% for flat-rate taxes. 'In at least some jurisdictions' and 'associated with' correctly hedge the claim to avoid overstating causation or universality.
explanations.A: Correct. The 19% vs. 11% average difference supports this hedged comparative claim without overclaiming universality (which would be undercut by the three low-permit-price exceptions).
explanations.B: Too strong — 'always' is directly undermined by the three jurisdictions where cap-and-trade showed no significant effect; in those cases, the flat-rate tax may have outperformed.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'universally' and 'regardless of permit price' is directly contradicted by the three low-price jurisdictions showing no significant reduction.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported — the data do not address flat-rate tax performance specifically in the three low-permit-price jurisdictions.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported — the data indicate cap-and-trade underperformed in low-permit-price jurisdictions, but no comparison to flat-rate tax performance in those specific jurisdictions is provided.
